extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, properties, and constructions for closed embeddings, locally closed embeddings, vanishing schemes, scheme-theoretic support and scheme-theoretic image in the language of schemes (with projective examples and exercises).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of closed embedding
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π : X → Y is a closed embedding (closed immersion) if it is affine and for every affine open Spec B ⊂ Y with π^{-1}(Spec B) ≅ Spec A, the map B → A is surjective (i.e., A ≅ B/I).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the local model of a closed subscheme. The text warns that the term 'embedding' is preferable to 'immersion' to avoid confusion with differential-geometric terminology. (See Def. 9.1.1 and related discussion.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed subscheme = isomorphism with closed embedding
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is a subset of Y and the map π is the inclusion on underlying sets, then X is a closed subscheme of Y; a closed embedding is equivalent to being isomorphic to such a closed subscheme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This connects the morphism notion (closed embedding) with the object notion (closed subscheme).

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed embedding induces homeomorphism onto closed subset (topology)
rubrics_metrics.description: A closed embedding identifies the topological space of X with a closed subset of the topological space of Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caution: the closed subset does not determine the closed subscheme — infinitesimal information (nonreduced 'fuzz') can be lost (e.g., Spec k[x] vs Spec k[x]/(x^2)). See Exercise 9.1.A and the cautionary examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed embeddings are finite and of finite type
rubrics_metrics.description: Closed embeddings are finite morphisms, and hence are morphisms of finite type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is stated as an 'easy exercise' (9.1.B) but is an important property used elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of closed embeddings
rubrics_metrics.description: The composition of two closed embeddings is a closed embedding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 9.1.C; useful when building complex embeddings from simpler ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affine-locality of closed embedding property
rubrics_metrics.description: The property of being a closed embedding is affine-local on the target.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 9.1.D: one can check closed-embedding-ness by restricting to an affine open cover of the target.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surjection of rings yields closed embedding on Specs
rubrics_metrics.description: If B → A is a surjection of rings, then the induced morphism Spec A → Spec B is a closed embedding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the prototypical local model: A ≅ B/I gives Spec A as closed subscheme Spec B/I.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed subschemes correspond to quasicoherent ideal sheaves
rubrics_metrics.description: A closed subscheme π : X → Y gives an exact sequence 0 → I_{X/Y} → O_Y → π_* O_X → 0 where I_{X/Y} is a quasicoherent sheaf of ideals; conversely, every quasicoherent sheaf of ideals on Y produces a closed subscheme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the sheaf-theoretic characterization (9.1.2 and 9.1.F). On affines the ideal sheaf restricts to the ideal I ⊂ B giving B/I. The exercises outline two approaches for constructing/gluing the closed subscheme from a quasicoherent ideal sheaf.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recovering closed subschemes by gluing affines
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a quasicoherent ideal sheaf I on Y, for each affine open Spec B the closed subscheme Spec B/I(B) glue compatibly to form the closed subscheme of Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 9.1.F provides two approaches: (1) check compatibility on overlaps and glue closed subschemes on affines; (2) describe X as a closed subset then define O_X via compatible germs and verify localization. Use distinguished opens to compare restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalent stalkwise surjectivity definition of closed embedding
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternate (usual in literature) definition: π : X → Y is a closed embedding if π induces a homeomorphism of underlying topological spaces onto a closed subset and the map π^#: O_Y → π_* O_X is surjective on stalks (i.e., surjective on rings on stalks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 9.1.H: show equivalence with the affine-local surjectivity definition (use that surjectivity of a morphism of sheaves can be checked on a suitable base).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scheme-theoretic unions and intersections of closed subschemes
rubrics_metrics.description: For closed subschemes given by ideals I_1, I_2 in an affine scheme, the scheme-theoretic union corresponds to I_1 ∩ I_2 (not I_1 I_2), and one can define scheme-theoretic intersection; underlying sets behave as set unions/intersections for finite unions and arbitrary intersections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 9.1.I(a) discusses choice of ideal for the union and warns about scheme-theoretic behavior differing from set-theoretic intuition (e.g., multiplicities and nonreduced structure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed embeddings are monomorphisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Closed embeddings (like open embeddings) are monomorphisms in the category of schemes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 9.1.J; used to deduce properties like compositions preserving monomorphisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of vanishing scheme V(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: For s ∈ Γ(Y, O_Y) a global section, the closed subscheme cut out by s (on affines Spec B take Spec B/(s|_{Spec B})) is the vanishing scheme V(s). For u invertible, V(s) = V(su); for S a set of functions define V(S).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 9.1.K gives the construction and basic properties; this is the scheme-theoretic analogue of zero loci.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scheme-theoretic support of a module/section
rubrics_metrics.description: If M is an A-module and m ∈ M, the scheme-theoretic support of m is Spec(A/Ann m). For a finitely generated module M, the scheme-theoretic support is defined as the intersection of closed subschemes Spec A/I for which M is an (A/I)-module (equivalently the union of supports of a finite generating set).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions and exercises 9.1.4, 9.1.L, 9.1.M show how to form supports and show the underlying set equals the usual set-theoretic support. Exercise 9.1.N globalizes this to quasicoherent sheaves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of locally closed embedding (locally closed immersion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π : X → Y is a locally closed embedding if it can be factored as X --ρ→ Z --τ→ Y with ρ a closed embedding and τ an open embedding (i.e., X is a closed subscheme of an open subscheme of Y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'immersion' is often used for this but is discouraged in the text (9.2 introduction). If X ⊂ Y as sets and π is inclusion, X is a locally closed subscheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locally closed embeddings are monomorphisms and locally of finite type
rubrics_metrics.description: Locally closed embeddings are monomorphisms and are locally of finite type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 9.2.A and remarks: composition of closed and open embeddings preserves monomorphism and finite type properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of locally closed embeddings
rubrics_metrics.description: The composition of two locally closed embeddings is again a locally closed embedding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 9.2.C: one may use factorizations and the relation between conditions (i),(ii),(iii) in Exercise 9.2.B to show this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalent/related descriptions of locally closed embeddings
rubrics_metrics.description: Three conditions for V ⊂ X: (i) V is intersection of an open subscheme and a closed subscheme; (ii) V is an open subscheme of a closed subscheme; (iii) V is a closed subscheme of an open subscheme (i.e., locally closed embedding). Conditions (i) and (ii) are equivalent and imply (iii); (iii) need not imply (i)/(ii) in pathological cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 9.2.B explains the equivalences and gives a diagrammatic (fibered product) viewpoint; refer to pathological counterexamples (Stacks, tag 01QW).

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed subschemes in projective space via homogeneous polynomials
rubrics_metrics.description: Any homogeneous polynomial (or collection thereof) in A[x_0,...,x_n] defines a closed subscheme of P^n_A by taking on each standard affine chart the vanishing of the dehomogenized polynomial(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 9.3.1: even if a homogeneous polynomial doesn't define a global function, its vanishing scheme is well-defined; Exercise 15.6.J (claimed) will show all closed subschemes of P^n_A are of this form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypersurfaces and degree in projective space
rubrics_metrics.description: A closed subscheme of P^n_k cut out by a single nonzero homogeneous polynomial is called a hypersurface; its degree is the degree of the polynomial. Special names: degree 1 hyperplane, degree 2 quadric, etc.; for n=2 call them curves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition 9.3.2 and remarks: degree is an intrinsic notion of the subscheme (to be justified later).

rubrics_metrics.name: Linear spaces and projective embeddings from graded rings
rubrics_metrics.description: Linear spaces in projective space are closed subschemes cut out by collections of linearly independent homogeneous linear polynomials. More generally, Proj of a finitely generated graded ring (generated in degree 1) can be embedded as a closed subscheme of some P^n_A via choosing generators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises 9.3.C, 9.3.F explain constructing linear spaces and describing Proj S as a closed subscheme of P^n when S is generated in degree 1; this underpins constructions like Veronese and twisted cubic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite morphisms are closed (via projective embedding)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π : X → Y is a finite morphism then π(X) is a closed subset of Y; proof via local reduction to the affine case, projectivity of X over Y, and the Fundamental Theorem of Elimination Theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 9.3.5 sketches the argument: reduce to Y=Spec B, show X is a projective B-scheme, then use elimination theory (Theorem 8.4.10) to conclude π(X) closed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of scheme-theoretic image
rubrics_metrics.description: The scheme-theoretic image of π : X → Y is the smallest closed subscheme Z ⊂ Y such that the composition I_{Z/Y} → O_Y → π_* O_X is zero; equivalently the intersection of all closed subschemes through which π factors (the intersection of closed subschemes containing the image).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition 9.4.2: in the affine case Y = Spec B the scheme-theoretic image is cut out by those functions in B which pull back to zero on X. Other names: closed subscheme-theoretic image, image closed subscheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior and examples of scheme-theoretic image (fuzz can persist/collapse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples show varied behavior: (1) fuzzy point Spec k[ε]/(ε^2) mapping into A^1 can give image Spec k[x]/(x^2) (fuzz persists); (2) fuzzy point mapping to 0 can give reduced image Spec k[x]/(x) (fuzz collapsed); (3) A^1 ackslash{0} → A^1 has scheme-theoretic image equal to all of A^1 even though set-theoretic image is A^1 ackslash{0}; (4) pathological examples exist where set-theoretic image is a point but scheme-theoretic image is whole Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These examples (in 9.4.2) illustrate that scheme-theoretic image captures algebraic/fuzz data and that the underlying set of the scheme-theoretic image is closed (often the closure of the set-theoretic image), but pathological behavior can occur without niceness hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affine-local criterion for computing scheme-theoretic image
rubrics_metrics.description: When the target Y is affine (Y = Spec B), the scheme-theoretic image is cut out by the ideal of functions g ∈ B whose pullback to X is zero; equivalently the kernel of the map B → Γ(X, O_X) (or to the coordinate ring of X in affine case).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 9.4.3 begins this affine-local discussion; examples 1–3 earlier illustrate this viewpoint explicitly.
